questions.title: Edema mechanism with low plasma albumin
questions.question: A patient presents with generalized edema. Investigations reveal low plasma albumin levels. Which of the following mechanisms is the primary cause of this patient's edema?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Raised capillary hydrostatic pressure is a separate mechanism of oedema (as in venous obstruction or heart failure), not the one driven by low plasma albumin.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Lymphatic obstruction produces a distinct, high-protein, non-pitting pattern of oedema (as in elephantiasis), not the mechanism linked to low plasma albumin.
explanations.C: Correct. Low plasma albumin lowers plasma colloidal (oncotic) osmotic pressure, the force that normally holds fluid in the capillaries and draws it back in at the venous end. With this osmotic pull weakened, filtration at the capillary wall outpaces reabsorption and fluid accumulates in the interstitium as generalised oedema — the mechanism behind hypoalbuminaemic states such as nutritional deficiency, liver cirrhosis and nephrotic syndrome.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Increased capillary permeability is the mechanism behind inflammatory oedema (from mediators such as histamine or kinins), not the mechanism specifically linked to low plasma albumin.

questions.learning_objective: State that low plasma albumin causes oedema by lowering plasma colloidal osmotic pressure.

questions.title: Precapillary sphincter relaxation trigger
questions.question: The precapillary sphincters at the beginning of capillaries relax primarily in response to:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Increased sympathetic tone constricts, rather than relaxes, precapillary sphincters and arterioles.
explanations.B: Correct. Precapillary sphincters relax primarily in response to the local accumulation of vasodilator metabolites (such as CO2, H+ and adenosine) and hypoxia that build up when tissue blood flow falls short of metabolic demand. This is the metabolic mechanism of local blood-flow autoregulation and active hyperaemia: a fall in flow causes metabolite accumulation, which dilates the arterioles and precapillary sphincters, restoring flow toward the tissue's needs.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Interstitial fluid osmotic pressure is a minor term in the Starling balance for fluid exchange, not the trigger for precapillary sphincter tone.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Plasma colloidal osmotic pressure governs fluid movement across the capillary wall, not the smooth-muscle tone of the precapillary sphincter itself.

questions.learning_objective: State that precapillary sphincters relax in response to local metabolite accumulation (metabolic autoregulation).

questions.title: General causes of oedema
questions.question: Edema can be caused by:

explanations.A: Correct. Increased capillary hydrostatic pressure is one of the four classic mechanisms of oedema. It arises from arteriolar dilation, venular constriction, raised venous pressure (from gravity, incompetent valves, venous obstruction or heart failure), or a raised total extracellular fluid volume. Any of these tips capillary filtration ahead of reabsorption and lymphatic drainage capacity, so fluid accumulates in the interstitium.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A raised, not increased, plasma protein concentration would raise colloidal osmotic pressure and oppose filtration; oedema follows from decreased, not increased, plasma protein concentration.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Decreased capillary hydrostatic pressure would favour reabsorption over filtration, the opposite of an oedema-producing change.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Decreased, not increased, capillary permeability would reduce fluid movement out of the vessel; increased permeability, not decreased, is an oedema-producing mechanism.

questions.learning_objective: Name increased capillary hydrostatic pressure as one of the classic mechanisms of oedema.
questions.module_subject: MUST-CVS-201 > Physiology > Capillary Circulation and Oedema > Mechanisms of Oedema

questions.title: Force absorbing fluid at the capillary venous end
questions.question: What is the primary force responsible for the absorption of fluid into the capillaries at the venous end?

options.C: Colloidal osmotic pressure of plasma proteins

explanations.A: Incorrect. Capillary hydrostatic pressure favours filtration (fluid moving out), not absorption; it falls along the capillary but never itself pulls fluid in.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Interstitial fluid osmotic pressure is a minor term in the Starling balance and, where it acts, favours filtration rather than absorption.
explanations.C: Correct. The colloidal (oncotic) osmotic pressure of plasma proteins, largely albumin, is the force that draws fluid back into the capillary. At the venous end, where capillary hydrostatic pressure has fallen well below its arteriolar-end value, this steady osmotic pull dominates the Starling balance and produces net absorption of fluid into the vessel.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Interstitial fluid hydrostatic pressure favours absorption only when it exceeds capillary pressure, which is not the primary mechanism this source names for venous-end absorption; the dominant force is plasma colloidal osmotic pressure.

questions.learning_objective: Name plasma colloidal osmotic pressure as the dominant force absorbing fluid at the capillary's venous end.

questions.title: Edema mechanism in deep vein thrombosis
questions.question: A patient presents with pitting edema in both lower limbs. Ultrasound reveals deep vein thrombosis. The edema in this case is primarily due to:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Decreased plasma proteins is the low-oncotic-pressure mechanism of oedema (as in nephrotic syndrome or liver disease), not the mechanism produced by venous obstruction.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Lymphatic obstruction produces a high-protein, non-pitting pattern (as in elephantiasis), not the pitting oedema described here, and DVT obstructs venous, not lymphatic, drainage.
explanations.C: Correct. Deep vein thrombosis obstructs venous outflow from the limb, raising venous pressure and, in turn, capillary hydrostatic pressure upstream of the obstruction. This tips the Starling balance toward filtration, producing the pitting oedema seen here — venous obstruction is one of the named causes of raised capillary hydrostatic pressure, alongside gravity-related venous pooling, incompetent valves and heart failure.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Increased capillary permeability is the inflammatory-mediator mechanism of oedema, not the mechanical venous-obstruction mechanism produced by a thrombus.

questions.learning_objective: Attribute the pitting oedema of DVT to increased capillary hydrostatic pressure from venous obstruction.

questions.title: Force driving filtration at the capillary arterial end
questions.question: Filtration at the arterial end of capillary occurs mainly due to:

explanations.A: Correct. At the arterial end of the capillary, capillary hydrostatic pressure is at its highest and exceeds the opposing plasma colloidal osmotic pressure, so the net Starling balance favours filtration — fluid moving out of the capillary into the interstitium. This hydrostatic pressure falls progressively toward the venous end, where the balance reverses toward absorption.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Interstitial hydrostatic pressure opposes filtration (it pushes fluid back toward the capillary), and is a minor term compared with capillary hydrostatic pressure in driving arterial-end filtration.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Capillary oncotic (colloidal osmotic) pressure opposes filtration by pulling fluid inward; it is not the force driving fluid out at the arterial end.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Interstitial oncotic pressure is usually very small and, where present, favours filtration only marginally; it is not the main driver named here, which is capillary hydrostatic pressure.

questions.learning_objective: Name capillary hydrostatic pressure as the dominant force driving filtration at the arterial end.

questions.title: Factors decreasing capillary filtration rate
questions.question: Which of the following tends to decrease capillary filtration rate?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Increased capillary hydrostatic pressure raises, not lowers, the outward filtration force and so increases filtration rate.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Decreased plasma colloid osmotic pressure weakens the inward-pulling force that opposes filtration, so it increases, not decreases, net filtration.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Increased interstitial colloid osmotic pressure would favour outward filtration further (drawing fluid into the interstitium), increasing rather than decreasing filtration rate.
explanations.D: Correct. Capillary filtration rate depends on the capillary filtration coefficient — the product of the wall's water permeability and the surface area available for exchange — as well as the Starling pressure gradient. A fall in capillary water permeability lowers this coefficient directly, decreasing filtration rate independent of any change in the hydrostatic or osmotic pressures themselves.

questions.learning_objective: Identify decreased capillary water permeability as a factor that lowers capillary filtration rate.

questions.title: Mechanism of electrolyte exchange across capillaries
questions.question: Which of the following mechanisms is most important for the exchange of electrolytes across capillaries?

explanations.A: Correct. Diffusion, driven by the concentration gradient and set by capillary permeability and molecular size, is quantitatively the most important mechanism of capillary exchange for small solutes such as electrolytes. Its rate depends on capillary permeability type, which increases across the sequence continuous (lowest) to fenestrated to discontinuous (highest) capillaries.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Bulk flow (the Starling-forces-driven filtration/reabsorption of fluid) moves water and small dissolved solutes together but is not the principal mechanism for electrolyte exchange specifically, which is dominated by diffusion.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Osmosis describes water movement driven by an osmotic gradient, not the primary mechanism by which electrolytes themselves cross the capillary wall.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Vesicular transport carries large, lipid-insoluble molecules such as proteins across the endothelium, not small electrolytes, whose exchange is dominated by diffusion instead.

questions.learning_objective: Name diffusion as the dominant mechanism of electrolyte exchange across the capillary wall.

questions.title: Edema mechanism in nephrotic syndrome
questions.question: A patient with nephrotic syndrome has significant proteinuria. The type of edema they develop is primarily due to:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Increased capillary permeability is a separate, inflammatory-mediator mechanism of oedema, not the loss-of-protein mechanism driving nephrotic-syndrome oedema.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Lymphatic obstruction is a mechanical drainage problem unrelated to proteinuria; nephrotic syndrome's oedema is not driven by lymphatic disease.
explanations.C: Correct. In nephrotic syndrome, heavy urinary protein loss lowers plasma albumin and so plasma colloidal osmotic pressure, the force that normally opposes capillary filtration and draws fluid back in at the venous end. With this osmotic pull weakened across the whole circulation, filtration outpaces reabsorption and generalised oedema develops — the same low-oncotic-pressure mechanism as other hypoalbuminaemic states such as liver cirrhosis or nutritional deficiency.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Increased capillary hydrostatic pressure describes the venous-congestion mechanism of oedema (as in heart failure or venous obstruction), not the low-protein mechanism of nephrotic syndrome.

questions.learning_objective: Attribute nephrotic-syndrome oedema to decreased plasma colloidal osmotic pressure from proteinuria.

questions.title: What vesicular transport carries across capillaries
questions.question: Vesicular transport across the capillary wall is primarily concerned with the movement of:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Water and electrolytes cross mainly by diffusion (and bulk flow for water), not by vesicular transport.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Small crystalloid solutes diffuse readily through capillary pores; they do not require the vesicular route.
explanations.C: Correct. Vesicular transport is a separate mechanism from diffusion that carries large, lipid-insoluble molecules — such as proteins, antibodies, cytokines and protein-bound hormones — across endothelial cells in membrane-bound vesicles. It supplies tissues with high-molecular-weight molecules that are too large to pass through ordinary capillary pores by diffusion.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Dissolved gases (O2, CO2) are small, lipid-soluble molecules that diffuse freely across the endothelium; they do not require vesicular transport.

questions.learning_objective: State that vesicular transport carries large, lipid-insoluble molecules such as proteins across the capillary wall.

questions.title: Pathophysiology of elephantiasis edema
questions.question: A patient with elephantiasis has massive edema in one leg. The underlying pathophysiology is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Increased capillary hydrostatic pressure produces a pitting, low-protein pattern of oedema (as in venous obstruction or heart failure), not the pattern seen in elephantiasis.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Decreased plasma colloidal osmotic pressure is the hypoalbuminaemic mechanism of oedema, unrelated to the lymphatic disease underlying elephantiasis.
explanations.C: Correct. Elephantiasis is the classic example of oedema from inadequate lymph flow. Chronic lymphatic obstruction, in this disease from filarial infection, causes oedema fluid with a high protein content rather than the low-protein fluid of filtration-driven oedema. In longstanding disease this produces non-pitting oedema with inflammation and fibrosis of the interstitial tissue, the massive, brawny swelling characteristic of elephantiasis.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Generalised salt and water retention (as in renal or heart failure) produces a different, more generalised oedema pattern, not the localised, fibrotic, lymphatic-obstruction pattern of elephantiasis.

questions.learning_objective: Attribute elephantiasis's massive, non-pitting oedema to chronic lymphatic obstruction.

questions.title: Force decreasing from the capillary arterial to venous end
questions.question: Which force, tending to move fluid out of the capillary, decreases significantly from the arterial end (35 mmHg) to the venous end (15 mmHg)?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Interstitial fluid osmotic pressure is usually very small and roughly constant along the capillary's length; it is not the outward force that falls sharply from arterial to venous end.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Colloidal osmotic pressure of plasma proteins is an inward-pulling (absorptive) force, not an outward-filtering one, and it stays comparatively steady along the capillary.
explanations.C: Correct. Capillary hydrostatic pressure is the outward-filtering force that falls markedly along the length of the capillary — from about 35 mmHg at the arterial end to about 15 mmHg at the venous end — because of the resistance the blood encounters flowing through the vessel. This fall is what shifts the Starling balance from net filtration at the arterial end to net absorption at the venous end.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Interstitial fluid hydrostatic pressure is an inward (absorptive) force, and is comparatively small and steady, not the outward force that falls from 35 to 15 mmHg along the capillary.

questions.learning_objective: Name capillary hydrostatic pressure as the outward Starling force that falls sharply from the arterial to the venous end.

questions.title: Edema from increased capillary hydrostatic pressure
questions.question: Which of the following is a cause of edema related to increased capillary hydrostatic pressure?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Proteinuria causes oedema by lowering plasma colloidal osmotic pressure (as in nephrotic syndrome), not by raising capillary hydrostatic pressure.
explanations.B: Correct. Right-sided heart failure raises systemic venous pressure as blood backs up behind the failing right ventricle. This raised venous pressure is transmitted upstream to raise systemic capillary hydrostatic pressure, producing the dependent, pitting peripheral oedema characteristic of right heart failure. It is one of the named causes of the raised-filtration-pressure mechanism of oedema, alongside venous obstruction and incompetent venous valves.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Filariasis causes oedema through lymphatic obstruction (as in elephantiasis), not through raised capillary hydrostatic pressure.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Left-sided heart failure raises pulmonary venous and capillary pressure, producing pulmonary oedema, rather than the systemic capillary hydrostatic-pressure rise this question asks about.

questions.learning_objective: Name right-sided heart failure as a cause of oedema via raised systemic capillary hydrostatic pressure.
